newsitem.title: UK: Russian eurobond talk of the town in London.
newsitem.headline: Russian eurobond talk of the town in London.

text.p: Bankers and investors on Friday flocked to attend a presentation by senior Russian officials to drum up support for the country's first Eurobond and many were impressed by what the heard.
"Everyone just wants to get their hands on Russian paper," said one Eurobond syndicate manager at a European bank who attended the meeting.
"Normally sovereign borrowers would be lucky to attract 50 investors to a roadshow. There were close to 450 here, which is unheard of."
London is the most international of the top financial centres and its investors are used to a steady stream of senior government officials passing through to boast about their economic progress.

But the scale and content of the affair went a long way towards swaying London's hard-to-please financial community. Russia's Eurobond marks the first time in 80 years that investors will be able to buy Russian debt and hold it overseas.
But some were disappointed they did not get to see Anatoly Chubais, President Boris Yeltsin's chief of staff.
Chubais was expected to attend, together with Finance Minister Alexander Livshits and other officials.
"A lot of people went because they were curious about seeing Chubais," said a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank, adding that the line-up was still quite impressive.
The presentation was held at The Brewery, a former brewery in London's financial district now used as a conference centre.
Precise terms of Russia's Eurobond were not given and officials said these would not be determined until after the global marketing blitz concluded in New York next week.

Top questions from the floor included the status of frozen MinFin bonds, tax collection, International Monetary Fund (IMF) negotiations, Tsarist bonds, Russia's privatisation programme and legal matters.
President Boris Yeltsin's health was not mentioned.
"Questions were asked about MinFin bonds, how long the backlog was for paying the army, IMF negotiations and Tsarist bonds," said one attendee. "But Yeltsin was not asked about at all."
Livshits, who left after half an hour to return to Moscow, gave a short talk pointing to the success of economic reforms.
Russian Deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov then gave a detailed analysis of the Russian economy in English.
Russian officials gave reassurances the frozen MinFin crisis was under control and they were taking measures to tackle arrears in public sector pay.
Tax collection was also a hot subject, but despite very detailed questions, bankers said the answers were vague and provided no new insights.
One indication of the success of the presentation was a more upbeat assessment of the potential pricing Russia would be able to secure for its Eurobond.
Spread talk was now between 300 and 335 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, down sharply from around 400 b.p. over a week ago, dealers said.
Officials at joint lead managers J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg declined to comment on the potential terms of the deal.
Traders said a $500 million five-year bond was widely expected, although official indications remained $300-$500 million and three to five years.
"I heard spread indications from bankers and fund managers of 300 to 335 b.p. over. On Thursday, it was 350 to 375 b.p. over and the day before it was 400 b.p. over.
"This would be very aggressive, but the sheer size of the roadshow attendance today makes it possible."
